```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

*mortensor is experimental software written largely with AI coding
assistants ("vibe-coded"). Use it at your own risk and check results
independently.*

mortensor builds probabilistic mortality forecasts: simulated paths of
future death rates, from which life expectancy, gaps between groups and
other quantities follow with their uncertainty. Any model can be used,
implemented in the package or wrapped from demography, StMoMo, StanMoMo or bamp,
and models can be combined. This vignette goes once through the main
steps with one simple model; the other vignettes take one step at a time.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
```

## 1. Data

`ons_data` holds deaths and mid-year populations in England by sex,
5-year age group and decile of the Index of Multiple Deprivation (decile 1
most deprived), 2001-2019 (Source: Office for National Statistics,
licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0). `mt_data()` reads them,
`mt_as_exposure()` takes the mid-year populations as person-years at risk,
and `mt_group_levels()` combines the deciles into quintiles:

```{r}
x <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile"), age = "age_group",
             value = c(deaths = "all_causes", population = "population"))
x <- mt_as_exposure(x, type = "midyear")
x <- mt_group_levels(x, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
x
```

`mt_validate()` checks the data for impossible values, gaps and
inconsistent totals:

```{r}
mt_validate(x)
```

## 2. The past

Life expectancy at birth by quintile, with Poisson intervals:

```{r}
mt_compare_forecasts(list(observed = x), periods = c(2001, 2019), strata = c("female.Q1", "female.Q5",
                                                                              "male.Q1", "male.Q5"))
```

## 3. A model and a forecast

Lee-Carter, fitted to each sex and quintile separately, as a simple
example. `mt_forecast()` simulates 500 paths of future death rates:

```{r}
fit <- mt_fit(lee_carter(), x)
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 15, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
fc
```

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 6}
mt_plot_forecast(fc, ages = c("50-54", "70-74", "85-89"), strata = c("female.Q1", "female.Q5"))
```

## 4. Results

Life expectancy is computed for every path, so its interval contains the
uncertainty of all ages together:

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_life_expectancy(fc, at = 0)
```

The gap between the least (Q5) and the most deprived quintile (Q1), also
path by path:

```{r, eval = has_gg}
gap <- mt_contrast(fc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", at = 0)
mt_plot_contrast(gap, observed = mt_contrast(x, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1"), levels = "Q5")
```

Separate Lee-Carter models continue each quintile's own trend, so the
female gap, which widened after 2011, keeps widening, with intervals that
grow quickly. Whether that is plausible is a question of model choice
("Choosing and combining models"); a model that pools the quintiles
behaves differently.

Other quantities work the same way: `asr()` (age-standardised rates),
`prob_dying()`, `mt_inequality()` (slope and relative index of
inequality), `mt_decompose()` (contributions of ages and causes to a gap).

## 5. Was the model any good?

A backtest fits the model to the years up to 2008, ..., 2014, forecasts
five years from each, and scores the forecasts against the observed rates:

```{r}
bt <- mt_compare(list("Lee-Carter" = lee_carter()), x, origins = 2008:2014, h = 5, n_draws = 200)
mt_score_table(bt, metrics = c("crps", "cov80", "cov95"))
```

The 95% intervals contained `r round(100 * mt_score(bt)$cov95)`% of the
observed rates, fewer than 95%: Lee-Carter's intervals are too narrow on
these data. "Backtesting and scores" explains the scores, "Tuning and
recalibration" how to widen the intervals.
